title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Jira to Plane, likely due to Plane's self-hosted and free option. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, with the key reason to switch being cost savings or data ownership.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Plane is free and self-hosted, while Jira has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Plane allows full data ownership since it's self-hosted, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical setup, while Jira offers a simpler, cloud-based setup.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large, enterprise teams, while Plane is more suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Easy to set up and use
* Native integration with Git
* Scalable for large teams
* Robust feature set
* Good customer support
### Plane
* Free and self-hosted
* Full data ownership
* Customizable
* Cost-effective
* Open-source community support
* Limited scalability
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited native integrations

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large, enterprise teams that need a robust feature set and native integration with Git. It's also a good choice for teams that don't mind paying a per-user monthly fee and want a simple, cloud-based setup. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for smaller to medium-sized teams that want a free, self-hosted option and full data ownership. It's also a good choice for teams that are technically savvy and want a customizable solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use a third-party import tool, such as the Plane import script, to import your data into Plane.
3. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira setup, including workflows and custom fields.
4. Test your Plane instance to ensure everything is working as expected.
5. Switch your team over to Plane and provide training on the new system.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the polish and features of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's API is still in development, which can make integrations with other tools more difficult. However, for teams that are technically savvy and want a free, self-hosted option, Plane is a good choice. We recommend switching to Plane if you're a small to medium-sized team that doesn't need all the features of Jira and wants to save on costs.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need native Git integration
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that want to save on costs and don't need advanced features
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and self-hosting
* Teams with simple project management needs that don't require a robust feature set
* Teams that are already using other open-source tools and want to integrate with Plane

## FAQ
### Can I use Plane for large, enterprise teams?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large, enterprise teams due to its limited scalability.
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, with no per-user monthly fees.
### Can I integrate Plane with Git?
Yes, Plane can be integrated with Git using third-party tools, but it's not a native integration like Jira.
### Is Plane open-source?
Yes, Plane is open-source and licensed under the Apache 2.0 license.
### Can I import my Jira data into Plane?
Yes, you can import your Jira data into Plane using a third-party import tool.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are cloud storage solutions that enable users to store, access, and share files from anywhere. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking for a reliable and secure file-sharing platform, especially those considering switching from a proprietary service to a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is file storage and collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership and control over their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user content.
* Setup complexity: Dropbox is generally easier to set up and use, with a more streamlined user interface, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Nextcloud is highly scalable, as users can increase storage capacity and add more users as needed, while Dropbox's scalability is limited by its pricing plans.
* Integration with other tools: Nextcloud has a built-in only office suite, while Dropbox integrates with Microsoft Office online.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $1996-$3316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with other tools and services
* Reliable and secure
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data and limited scalability
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosted and open-source, giving users full control over their data
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Integrates well with other open-source tools
* Free to use, with costs limited to server maintenance
* Can be complex to set up and require technical expertise

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use file-sharing solution and are willing to pay a monthly fee per user. It's also a good option for individuals who want to collaborate with others and don't require a high level of control over their data. On the other hand, Nextcloud is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require a high level of scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's also a good choice for users who value open-source software and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox files in ZIP format using the Dropbox website or desktop client.
2. Set up a Nextcloud server, either on your own hardware or through a hosting provider.
3. Use the Nextcloud web interface to import your ZIP file and set up your account.
4. Configure any additional settings, such as user accounts and permissions, as needed.
5. Test your Nextcloud setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high level of scalability, customization, and control over data. However, it's worth noting that Nextcloud can be complex to set up and require technical expertise, which may be a barrier for some users. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's built-in office suite may not be as polished as some proprietary alternatives. We recommend switching to Nextcloud for users who value open-source software and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10-20 users who don't require a high level of integration with proprietary tools
* Large teams of 100+ users who need a scalable and customizable solution
* Individuals who value open-source software and are willing to invest time into setting up and maintaining their own server
* Teams who require a high level of control over their data and don't need phone support
* Organizations with existing IT infrastructure and expertise who can self-host Nextcloud

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance.
### Is Nextcloud as easy to use as Dropbox?
No, Nextcloud can be more complex to set up and use, especially for non-technical users.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other tools and services?
Yes, Nextcloud has a wide range of integrations with other open-source tools and services.
### Is my data safe with Nextcloud?
Yes, Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership and control over their data, and offers a high level of security and encryption.
### Can I migrate my Dropbox files to Nextcloud?
Yes, you can export your Dropbox files in ZIP format and import them into Nextcloud.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers more control and scalability than Dropbox. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two popular tools used for database management and team collaboration. Both tools offer a range of features that benefit teams of various sizes, from small startups to large enterprises. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and customizable database solution, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan with limited features, while NocoDB is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows for full data ownership, while Airtable stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and is easier to set up, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: NocoDB is highly scalable, while Airtable can become expensive for large teams.
* Feature difference: NocoDB offers a built-in SQL editor, while Airtable relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Airtable
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations and templates
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
* Can become expensive for large teams
### NocoDB
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Full data ownership and control
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited support resources

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a user-friendly and easy-to-set-up database solution. It's ideal for teams that don't require full data ownership and are willing to pay for the convenience of a proprietary solution. NocoDB, on the other hand, is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require high scalability and full control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams with technical expertise and a desire for a free and open-source solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Airtable data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a new NocoDB instance, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to upload your exported data.
4. Configure your NocoDB instance to match your Airtable setup, including any necessary integrations or templates.
5. Test your NocoDB instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and user-friendliness of Airtable. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that NocoDB's SQL editor can be finicky and requires a good understanding of SQL syntax. However, for teams that require full data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing their database solution, NocoDB is a clear winner.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with simple database needs that don't require Airtable's premium features
* Medium-sized teams with growing database needs that want to reduce costs
* Large teams with complex database needs that require high scalability
* Teams with strict data ownership requirements
* Developers who want a free and open-source database solution

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between Airtable and NocoDB?
The main difference is that Airtable is a proprietary solution with limited data ownership, while NocoDB is a free and open-source solution with full data ownership.
### Can I self-host NocoDB?
Yes, NocoDB can be self-hosted on your own servers.
### Is NocoDB suitable for small teams?
Yes, NocoDB can be suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and customize.
### Can I migrate my Airtable data to NocoDB?
Yes, you can export your Airtable data in CSV or JSON format and import it into NocoDB.
### Is NocoDB production-ready?
Not yet, as it still lacks some of the polish and user-friendliness of Airtable.
